entries.note: To linguists, accent covers only differences in pronunciation, so it is a narrower term than [[see:dialect]], which can include it.
Covers differences between varieties at every level, including syntax, vocabulary and pronunciation, so it takes in [[see:accent]].
Its two pronunciations are given as an example of a difference in [[see:accent]].
Set against 'we were' as an example of a syntactic difference between varieties, which is part of [[see:dialect]].
One US regional word for a soft drink, alongside [[see:pop]] and [[see:soda]], showing a vocabulary difference in [[see:dialect]].
One US regional word for a soft drink, alongside [[see:Coke]] and [[see:soda]], showing a vocabulary difference in [[see:dialect]].
One US regional word for a soft drink, alongside [[see:Coke]] and [[see:pop]], showing a vocabulary difference in [[see:dialect]].
People argue over its pronunciation: three syllables in the US South and New England, two in the Midwest and West, a regional case of [[see:syllable reduction]].
In fast everyday speech its vowels weaken or drop, an example of natural [[see:syllable reduction]] and the [[see:schwa]].
Discussed in a previous episode; three- and four-syllable pronunciations have coexisted since it was borrowed, much like [[see:caramel]].
Dropping a syllable, which is common in words over two syllables and especially in English, where unstressed syllables get the weak [[see:schwa]].
The vowel English unstressed syllables often take, a weakened form of the original vowel that makes it easy to drop altogether.
R-dropping started as lower-class English speech, was called a vulgar provincialism in the 1700s, became posh in London by the late 1800s, and New Englanders then copied it.
The posh London accent with R-dropping and a broad 'ah' vowel, which has only been the prestige model for about 200 years.
An R-dropped form of [[from:burst]], found in 1600s writing, when R began disappearing before S sounds.
The form with the R that gave [[gave:bust]] when R began dropping before S in the 1600s.
An early R-dropped form of [[from:parcel]], recorded in 1600s writing.
The difference between it and [[from:arse]] comes from early R-dropping before S sounds.
The R-ful form behind [[gave:ass]].
An R-dropped version of [[from:cursing]], from the same early loss of R before S sounds.
The form with the R that gave [[gave:cussing]].
The technical term for R after a vowel, as in 'cart' and 'car', which was dropped wholesale in England by the late 1800s.
Compared with [[see:autumn]] as a word kept in American English, which feeds the myth that Americans sound like Shakespeare.
The British counterpart of American [[see:fall]].
Sounds the same as [[see:marry]] and [[see:merry]] for most Americans, a merger that Shakespeare's English did not have.
Merged with [[see:Mary]] and [[see:merry]] in American English, which shows American speech is not Shakespearean.
Merged with [[see:Mary]] and [[see:marry]] in American English, which shows American speech is not Shakespearean.
Sounds the same as [[see:fur]] in American English, an example of vowels merging before R.
Merged with [[see:fir]] in American English.
Sounds the same as [[see:hoarse]] for Americans, though they would have differed in Shakespeare's time.
Merged with [[see:horse]] in American English.
An older relic form still used in Britain, where Americans say [[see:guess]], though Tennesseans kept it too.
What Americans say where the British [[see:reckon]].
The widespread myth that [[see:Appalachian English]] is Shakespeare's English, which probably arose to counter the region being disparaged as uneducated.
Kept some archaic British features, such as [[see:a-prefixing]], that other American varieties lost, but it does not sound like Shakespeare.
The older 'a-fishing, a-hunting' construction, a salient feature of [[see:Appalachian English]] that young speakers have largely dropped.
Picking up words like this and [[see:bloody]] after moving to Britain makes you sound instantly, but not authentically, British.
Given with [[see:blimey]] as a word that makes a newcomer sound superficially British.
Its stereotyped New York pronunciation is a one-off that a newcomer can pick up quickly without acquiring the accent.
The stereotyped New York 'cawfee' reflects a wider vowel pattern tied to the [[see:cot–caught merger]], and incomers adopt it first.
Widespread in the US and Canada but absent in New York and Britain; Canadians in New York partly unmerged these vowels after five years.
Paired with [[see:hawk]] as historically separate vowels that fall together under the [[see:cot–caught merger]].
Paired with [[see:hock]] as an example of the [[see:cot–caught merger]].
Paired with [[see:collar]] as an example of the [[see:cot–caught merger]].
Paired with [[see:caller]] as an example of the [[see:cot–caught merger]].
Valerie's term for someone who has moved and cobbled together features of an old and a new accent, sounding like neither.
Immigrants' grandchildren speak the new place's language and lose the old one, which is why immigrant languages don't overwhelm English and Native American languages die out.
Worried that German speakers would damage English, a fear the [[see:three-generation pattern]] shows was groundless.
The movement of African Americans to the North in the early 1900s, one of the migrations that reshaped American accents.
The idea that sounds themselves are appealing or off-putting; sonorant-rich languages are favoured, but familiarity matters far more.
Widespread hatred of words like [[see:moist]], [[see:panties]] and [[see:crud]], which is driven partly by their meaning and perhaps by their sounds.
A famously hated word, a classic example of [[see:word aversion]].
A hated word with sexual associations; Valerie's friend said they couldn't be friends if she ever used it.
A hated word, usually for something gross, showing that [[see:word aversion]] can come from meaning.
Often called the most beautiful English phrase because it is full of vowels, L and R, the [[see:sonorant]] sounds people prefer.
The company behind the British [[see:Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?]], named after [[from:cellar door]] in a non-rhotic spelling.

entries.term: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?
entries.note: The British version was produced by [[see:Celador]].
Sounds made with an open, singable articulation, such as vowels, L, R, N, M and glides, which phonaesthetic studies find most pleasing.
A syllable ending in a vowel; languages full of them, such as French, Italian and Spanish, are often called beautiful.
Cited as a horrific word by [[see:open syllable]] standards, showing English isn't phonaesthetically pleasing.
A name for the singable, melodious, sexy quality of languages like French and Italian.
Describes languages like Italian, French and Spanish, which give every syllable roughly equal weight and are rated more attractive than [[see:stress-timed]] ones.
Describes languages like English, German and Russian, which cram unstressed syllables between stresses and so reduce vowels.
Rob jokes that English is nicer 'when we iamb our pentameters', a pun on [[see:stress-timed]] rhythm.
A British accent that gets little love; listeners unfamiliar with British accents rate it against [[see:received pronunciation]] arbitrarily.
A language of Senegal with strong French influence; outsiders could pick out its prestige varieties, perhaps by recognising the French.
Its American, Cockney and southern British pronunciations all weaken a sound, yet only some are judged badly, showing that prestige is arbitrary.
Says 'water' with a [[see:glottal stop]] and is judged lazy, though posh R-dropping is an even greater weakening.
The trilled Scottish R, probably like the historical English R from which today's weaker British and American Rs developed.
A sound made by closing the glottis; in [[see:Cockney]] 'water' it replaces T, which weakens the T rather than dropping it.
